subject: Arabic
source: Drive: Curriculum/Arabic folder and Secondary Lesson Plan - Arabic - Y8 (format and approach); National Curriculum early language learning

lessons.title: My mother and my father
objectives: Say mother and father in Arabic
Say 'This is my mother' and 'This is my father'
Show respect and kindness to parents
starter: How do you say 'as-salaamu alaykum' and the reply?
How do you say 'my name is ...' in Arabic?
Count from one to five in Arabic.

teach.heading: Bismillah and our families
bullets: Today we talk about our family
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and as-salaamu alaykum. Ask: who lives in your house? Pupils may share names; accept any family shape sensitively (some pupils live with grandparents or one parent). Say 'usra' and have pupils echo.

teach.heading: My mother
teach.note: Show a picture of a mother and child. Teach ummee with a heart gesture. Explain that haadhihi is used for a girl or woman. Pupils repeat the sentence. Avoid grammatical terms; use gestures: point to a girl/woman picture.

teach.heading: My father
teach.note: Contrast haadhaa for a man or boy. Quick game: show male/female pictures and pupils choose haadhaa or haadhihi. Common error: swapping haadhaa and haadhihi - correct gently and repeat.

teach.heading: I love
teach.note: Introduce uhibbu as 'I love'. Sentence: uhibbu ummee, uhibbu abee. Discuss why we love and respect parents. The Qur'an tells us to be kind to parents (Qur'an 17:23, plain statement that we should be good to parents). Keep this short.

teach.heading: Pairs and lines
teach.note: Add 'wa' meaning 'and' (wa abee). Practise reading a model sentence from the board together. Use hand signs: right hand for ummee, left for abee, as a memory aid.

practice: Teacher shows a picture of a mother; pupils say 'haadhihi ummee'.
Teacher shows a picture of a father; pupils say 'haadhaa abee'.
Match the picture of a mother or father to the correct Arabic sentence.
Say 'uhibbu ummee' and 'uhibbu abee' to a partner.
independent: Draw your mother and father and label with ummee and abee.
Write the sentence 'haadhihi ummee' under your mother's picture.
Colour in the hearts and say 'uhibbu ummee wa abee'.
exit: Do we say haadhaa or haadhihi for a father?
lessons.homework: Tell your parents 'uhibbu ummee' / 'uhibbu abee' and tell us what they said.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards for mother and father with large Arabic text; use gestures. EAL: write the home-language word beside the Arabic. Stretch: write the sentence 'uhibbu ummee wa abee' in Arabic letters by copying.

lessons.title: Brothers, sisters and grandparents
objectives: Say brother, sister, grandfather and grandmother in Arabic
Describe a family picture using short sentences
starter: How do you say 'my mother' in Arabic?
How do you say 'this is my father' in Arabic?

teach.heading: Recap the family
teach.note: Quick recap using the picture cards. Ask: haadhaa or haadhihi for a man? Make this fast and fun: show a card and pupils whisper the answer, then shout it.

teach.heading: Brother and sister
teach.note: Model both words. Misconception: pupils confuse akhee and ukhtee as they sound alike. Teach a hook: 'akh' is like a boy 'ahh!' and 'ukht' ends with a 't' like 'sister'. Practise in pairs with picture cards.

teach.heading: Grandparents
teach.note: Introduce the new words with pictures. Talk about respecting grandparents. Ask pupils to show how they greet grandparents (salaam, kissing the hand is cultural - say 'with kindness'). Keep the discussion inclusive.

teach.heading: Making sentences
teach.note: Read together slowly, pointing to each word right to left. Explain 'wa' joins words. Pupils clap on each word to feel the rhythm.

teach.heading: Our family tree
bullets: Say the Arabic under each person
teach.note: Model drawing a family tree with simple circles on the board; label with Arabic. Ask pupils which family members they have. Allow pupils to leave out members and add others (aunties, uncles) using English.

practice: Show the picture of a mother and father and say the Arabic words.
Match four picture cards (brother, sister, grandfather, grandmother) to the Arabic words.
Say 'haadhaa akhee' while pointing to a picture of a brother.
independent: Draw your own family tree with at least four people and label the people in Arabic.
Say three sentences about your family using haadhaa/haadhihi.
Practise 'uhibbu akhee wa ukhtee' with a partner.
exit: Say 'This is my sister' in Arabic.
lessons.homework: Draw or print a family photo and label each person in Arabic or English-Arabic mix. Show it next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards, limit to two new words at a time. EAL: write family words in the home language. Stretch: write 'haadhaa jaddee wa haadhihi jaddatee' by copying and read it aloud.

lessons.title: Colours around us
objectives: Name the colour of an object in Arabic
Notice the beauty of Allah's creation
starter: How do you say 'my brother' in Arabic?
How do you say 'my grandmother' in Arabic?

teach.heading: Colours
teach.note: Show coloured cards. Teach each with an object: apple (ahmar), sky (azraq), leaf (akhdar). Pupils echo twice. Misconception: 'akhdar' has the throaty kh sound - model it clearly.

teach.heading: More colours
teach.note: Use examples: sun (asfar), milk (abyad), night sky or the Kaaba's covering (aswad). Mention carefully: the Kiswah covering the Kaaba is black. Pupils say each colour when you flash the card.

teach.heading: What colour is it?
teach.note: Teach 'maa lawnuhu?' as a question. Ask about objects: What colour is the apple? Pupils answer in Arabic. Accept English if they cannot recall; then repeat the Arabic.

teach.heading: Colour and creation
bullets: Look at the sky, plants and flowers
teach.note: Take a moment to appreciate creation: show pictures of a rainbow, flowers, a green garden. Qur'an 30:22 mentions the diversity of our languages and colours as a sign - say 'Allah made us different and beautiful'. Keep it simple.

teach.heading: Colour game
bullets: Hold it up to the camera
teach.note: Play 'colour hunt': say an Arabic colour; pupils find an item of that colour at home within 10 seconds. Praise effort; do not penalise lack of available items.

practice: Say 'haadhaa abee' and 'haadhihi ummee' for pictures.
Match the Arabic family word to the picture: akhee, ukhtee, jaddee, jaddatee.
Match colour cards to the Arabic colour words.
Ask your partner 'maa lawnuhu?' about a toy; answer with an Arabic colour.
Colour in a picture of a rainbow and label two colours in Arabic.
independent: Colour the shapes and write the Arabic colour word underneath: red apple, blue sea, green leaf.
Find three objects in your room and say their colours in Arabic.
Draw a flag and say its colours in Arabic.
exit: How do you ask 'What colour is it?' in Arabic?
lessons.homework: Find five things at home and tell us their colours in Arabic.
lessons.send: SEND: use colour swatches and objects; reduce to four colours at first. EAL: label each colour in the home language. Stretch: say 'ahmar wa abyad' for objects with two colours.

lessons.title: Letters: Jeem, Haa and Khaa
objectives: Recognise the shapes and sounds of ج ح خ
Say a word that begins with each letter
Notice where the dot is placed

keywords.def: a letter with a dot below the belly, sound 'j'
a letter with no dot, a breathy 'h' from the throat
a letter with a dot above, a throaty 'kh'

starter: Which letters did we learn: alif, baa and ...?
How many dots are under baa?
How do you say 'red' in Arabic?

teach.heading: Revision and new letters
bullets: أ ب ت - alif, baa, taa
teach.note: Do a rapid recap of alif, baa, taa using flashcards. Then show jeem, Haa, khaa and say they are 'cousins' because they share a body shape and differ by the dot. Ask pupils to spot the dots.

teach.heading: Jeem ج
teach.note: Walk like a camel (hump hump) and say jamal. Show the dot underneath inside the curve. Pupils trace the shape in the air. Misconception: some pupils say 'zh' or 'g'; model a clear 'j' like jam.

teach.heading: Haa ح
teach.note: Teach the breath sound: fog a mirror or breathe on your hand. Gallop like a horse and say hisaan. Compare with English 'h' - it is deeper. No dot is the key clue.

teach.heading: Khaa خ
teach.note: Make a gentle throaty sound like clearing the throat softly. Say khubz and mime eating bread. Ask: where is the dot - above or below?

teach.heading: Which one is it?
teach.note: Use a quick-fire game: say the sound and pupils hold up a card or draw the shape on a whiteboard. Ask: which letter has the dot above? Reinforce by tracing each shape three times.

practice: Hold up alif, baa, taa cards for sounds.
Say 'ahmar' and 'azraq' with the matching colours.
Look at three cards (ج ح خ) and say the sound; teacher checks each.
Match picture to letter: camel, horse, bread.
Trace each letter in the air saying the sound.
independent: Trace ج ح خ on a worksheet and say a word for each.
Draw a camel, a horse and a loaf and write the first letter beside each.
Ask a partner: 'Which letter has the dot above?' (khaa).
exit: Which is the first sound of khubz?
lessons.homework: Write each of the letters ج ح خ three times and draw a picture for each.
lessons.send: SEND: raised or large letters, trace on a tablet. EAL: link sounds to home-language sounds if similar. Stretch: spot the letter ج or خ in the Arabic text on a worksheet.
